source.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Chinchilla Compute-Optimal Scaling
source.authors: Rylan Schaeffer; Noam Levi; Andreas Kirsch; Theo Guenais; Brando Miranda; Elyas Obbad; O. Koyejo

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study re-fits Chinchilla’s scaling analysis under alternative parameter counts and structured perturbations. Its results mostly confirm robustness, but show that some parameter-count errors can change the inferred compute-optimal trend.
record.gate_note: The paper reanalyzes Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model data; it does not train new language models or independently test the fit against alternative functional forms. Results cited from prior studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study re-fits Chinchilla's own loss data with the same parametric form and fitting code (Besiroglu et al.) under three parameter-count definitions and four synthetic perturbations. It reports the fitted L(N,D) parameters and the compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio. This bears directly on V3 (compute-optimal split) and V7 (dependence on parameter counting). It trains no new models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Authors conclude Chinchilla's fit and ≈20 tokens/parameter prescription are robust to the three parameter-count interpretations; the standard formula makes the ratio even flatter. Multiplicative errors and noise have limited effects, while additive or systematic errors can alter the ratio's flat trend. Overall the key results withstand sizable perturbations.
record.recipe_differences: Re-fits Chinchilla’s published loss data using Besiroglu et al. (2024)’s fitting code, then varies parameter-count definitions and applies four structured perturbations; it does not reproduce the original training runs.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with parameter-count interpretation and perturbation type. Additive constants and systematic biases can change the compute trend; multiplicative constants shift the ratio level; log-normal noise increases uncertainty and can make fits unidentifiable.

fits_no_version.finding: Chinchilla Table A9 reported parameter counts disagree with a standard architecture formula for 50/50 models (mean 7.4%, max 15.2%). A 'best fit' formula with 5× attention parameters matches 44/50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Published parameter counts in scaling-law studies can be ambiguous or irreproducible from the stated architecture.

record.problems: The analysis reuses Chinchilla’s data rather than training independent runs; compute-optimal allocations are inferred from fitted loss laws rather than directly compared across compute-matched training runs. Several plotted outcomes are described qualitatively rather than reported as exact values.

untested.parts: All: no goodness-of-fit test of the power-law form, no new runs, no separate test against compute.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
No IsoFLOP or compute-matched training comparison; only Chinchilla Approach-3-style parametric fit. No test of the Kaplan-style allocation.
Sensitivity to training schedule, data, fitting method/loss, and curve bending are not tested. Only parameter counting (real and synthetic perturbations) is tested.

missing.what: Analytic derivation that a multiplicative count error shifts the optimal ratio by ≈c_m^−1 without changing its compute exponent. Systematic bias changes the exponent to (α/s−β)/(α/s+β).
Ê rises only ~21% (1.565→1.897) while B̂, β̂ show no trend under additive perturbation. Currently only in the R8 note, which mixes it with the positive-constant condition.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the tranche from T5 to T1: the study is a same-data, same-method re-fit that mostly confirms Chinchilla, not a challenge. I removed the reader's V1 'supports' label, since no power-law adequacy is tested. I reversed the reader's V7 'supports' label for R1–R5: robustness to counting is evidence against fit-dependence in that condition. The perturbations are synthetic, applied to standard-formula counts, not actual alternative measurements. Appendix C.2.3's description of s<1 contradicts Sec. 3.3. The text gives a σ sweep of 0.01–100, but figure legends show 0–3.162.

versions.untested_parts: The paper re-fits the Chinchilla pretraining-loss scaling law under alternative parameter counts, but does not independently establish power-law adequacy, test loss against compute as a separate variable, or validate the claim across new runs.
No test of predictions from small runs against substantially larger runs.
The compute-optimal allocation is derived from fitted Chinchilla scaling laws; the study does not directly train and compare compute-matched runs to find the empirical minimum.
No comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architectural choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested.
The study tests sensitivity to parameter-count definitions and four structured parameter-count perturbations, but not sensitivity to training schedule, data, or alternative fitting procedures.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)
rows.size_stated: 44M to 16B parameters (range stated for the original Chinchilla models)
rows.operation_detail: Re-fit the Chinchilla pretraining-loss scaling law using three alternative parameter-count interpretations.

conditions.value: reported, standard formula, or best-fit formula

rows.measure: Fitted scaling-law parameters Ê, Â, α̂, B̂, β̂
rows.value: The five fitted parameters did not differ significantly across the three parameter-count interpretations.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors from 4000 bootstrap samples; exact values not stated in text.
rows.note: The fitted form is L(N,D) = E + A·N^−α + B·D^−β. This is a re-fit of Chinchilla data, not a new independent test of whether that form is adequate.
rows.check: Unlink V1: the re-fit assumes the power-law form and reports no goodness of fit, so it cannot show whether loss falls as a power law. For V7 the state is absent, not observed: the five fit parameters did not differ significantly across counts that differ by up to 15.2%.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)
rows.size_stated: 44M to 16B parameters (range stated for the original Chinchilla models)
rows.operation_detail: Recompute the fitted compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio using reported model parameter counts.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal tokens per parameter and its slope per 10× increase in compute
rows.value: Ratio remains around 20; slope −1.248 per decade of compute.
rows.uncertainty: 80% confidence intervals; exact values not stated in text.
rows.note: The ratio is described as remaining constant around 20, but this is the steepest of the three reported slopes.
rows.check: For V3 this should be observed, not partial. Authors say the ratio stays constant around 20 and that uncertainty prevents strong conclusions about slope differences (−1.248 vs −0.572). For V7 it is absent (no meaningful change); the units of the 'slope per decade' are unclear in the text.

source_check.correct: V3: observed. V7: absent; ordinary counting interpretations do not meaningfully change the results. Reported-count ratio remains around 20, with slope −1.248 per decade.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2, Figure 2 caption and accompanying paragraph.
source_check.problem: The shared observed state fits V3 but not V7.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)
rows.size_stated: 44M to 16B parameters (range stated for the original Chinchilla models)
rows.operation_detail: Refit after multiplying every standard-formula parameter count by a constant.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter trend and fitted ratio magnitude
rows.value: The ratio remains constant with compute, while its constant level shifts with the multiplier; underestimation raises it and overestimation lowers it.
rows.uncertainty: 80% confidence intervals; exact values not stated in text.
rows.note: The paper states that the ratio’s constant changes as a power of the multiplier.
rows.check: For V3 the state is observed (ratio flat with compute). For V7 it is partial: only the ratio's level shifts (≈c_m^-1 per Appendix C.2.1) and α̂ is unchanged. The perturbation is synthetic, applied to standard-formula counts.

source_check.correct: V3: observed where identifiable. V7: partial; the ratio level and model-size prefactor change, while the exponent and approximately flat compute trend remain stable. The two smallest multipliers, 0.001 and approximately 0.004, produce NaNs.
source_check.problem: The shared observed state overstates V7 dependence; extreme multipliers also have undefined ratio estimates.

rows.operation_detail: Refit after multiplying every standard-formula parameter count by a very small constant.
rows.value: NaNs produced because of uncertainty in Â and α̂.
rows.note: The ratio could not be inferred for these two settings.
rows.check: No fix needed; ratio not inferable (NaNs) at c_m = 0.001 and 0.004.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)
rows.size_stated: 44M to 16B parameters (range stated for the original Chinchilla models)
rows.operation_detail: Refit after adding the same constant to every standard-formula parameter count.
rows.measure: Fitted parameter exponent α̂ and compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter trend
rows.value: For negative constants, α̂ is below its unperturbed value; larger compute budgets require fewer tokens per parameter.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors from 4000 bootstrap samples for fit parameters; ratio has 80% confidence intervals. Exact intervals not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports the direction of the trend for negative additive constants, not a separate numerical slope for this condition group.
rows.check: Condition range is wrong: the sweep is −logspace(6.6,7.6,5), i.e. −4.0e6 to −4.0e7, not −7.1e6. For V3 it is partial: the ratio trends downward with compute, so equal N/D growth breaks under synthetic additive error. For V7 it is observed.

source_check.correct: Negative constants are −logspace(6.6,7.6,5), approximately −4.0e7 to −4.0e6. Negative offsets lower the fitted parameter exponent and make the optimal ratio decrease with compute. V3: partial; V7: observed.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Equation 7 and following paragraphs; Figure 5 top right.
source_check.problem: The negative sweep endpoint is wrong, and partial does not describe the observed V7 dependence.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)
rows.size_stated: 44M to 16B parameters (range stated for the original Chinchilla models)
rows.operation_detail: Refit after adding the same constant to every standard-formula parameter count.
rows.measure: Fitted parameter exponent α̂ and compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter trend
rows.value: Across the full sweep, α̂ increases from 0.199 to 0.481; positive constants make larger compute budgets require more tokens per parameter.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors from 4000 bootstrap samples for fit parameters; ratio has 80% confidence intervals. Exact intervals not stated.
rows.note: The paper also reports Ê rising from 1.565 to 1.897 across the full additive-constant sweep.
rows.check: Condition range should be 4.0e6 to 4.0e7. The value 'α̂ 0.199 to 0.481' and 'Ê 1.565 to 1.897' span the full sweep including negative constants, not only the positive group. For V3 partial; for V7 observed (α̂ shifts strongly with additive counting error).

source_check.correct: Positive constants are logspace(6.6,7.6,5), approximately 4.0e6 to 4.0e7. The exponent range 0.199–0.481 and irreducible-loss range 1.565–1.897 span the full negative-to-positive sweep. Positive offsets raise the exponent relative to baseline and make the optimal ratio increase with compute. V3: partial; V7: observed.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2; Figure 4 second row; Figure 5 top right.
source_check.problem: The positive sweep endpoint is wrong; full-sweep numerical ranges are attached to a positive-only condition; V7 should be observed.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)
rows.size_stated: 44M to 16B parameters (range stated for the original Chinchilla models)
rows.operation_detail: Refit after applying a systematic size-dependent bias to standard-formula parameter counts.
rows.measure: Fitted parameter exponent α̂ and compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter trend
rows.value: α̂ follows α̂ = 10^−0.46 · s^−1; for s < 1, larger compute budgets require more tokens per parameter.
rows.uncertainty: Fit reported as R² > 0.999, p ≈ 5.9 × 10^−90; ratio has 80% confidence intervals.
rows.note: The paper says the fit parameters Ê, B̂, and β̂ show no systematic trend in this perturbation.
rows.check: For V3 partial (ratio rises with compute when s<1). For V7 observed: α̂ = 10^−0.46·s^−1, R²>0.999. Appendix C.2.3 describes s<1 inconsistently with Sec. 3.3; Sec. 3.3 and the formula say s<1 compresses the range.

source_check.correct: V3: partial. V7: observed. The fitted exponent follows α̂ = 10^−0.46·s^−1, with R² > 0.999 and p approximately 5.9×10^−90; for s < 1, the optimal ratio increases with compute.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, Equation 8 and following paragraphs; Figure 5 bottom left.
source_check.problem: Partial fits V3's equal-growth prescription but understates the observed V7 dependence.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)

rows.measure: Fitted parameter exponent α̂ and compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter trend
rows.value: α̂ decreases as s increases; for s > 1, larger compute budgets require fewer tokens per parameter.

rows.note: The paper says the fit parameters Ê, B̂, and β̂ show no systematic trend in this perturbation.
rows.check: For V3 partial (ratio falls with compute when s>1). For V7 observed.

source_check.correct: V3: partial. V7: observed. The fitted exponent decreases inversely with s; for s > 1, the optimal ratio decreases with compute.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3; Figure 4 third row; Figure 5 bottom left.
source_check.problem: Partial fits V3's equal-growth prescription but understates the observed V7 dependence.

rows.subject: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla model set (50 models)
rows.size_stated: 44M to 16B parameters (range stated for the original Chinchilla models)
rows.operation_detail: Refit after applying log-normal noise independently to parameter counts.
rows.measure: Uncertainty in fitted parameters and compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter trend
rows.value: Fit-parameter confidence intervals generally widen with noise; the ratio’s inferred values increase and its uncertainty grows by approximately 1 order of magnitude, while the ratio remains roughly constant with compute when identifiable.
rows.uncertainty: Standard errors from 4000 bootstrap samples; ratio has 80% confidence intervals.
rows.note: The paper reports that Â and α̂ nearly lose identifiability at σ = 3.162.
rows.check: For V3 observed: inferred ratio roughly constant with compute where identifiable. For V7 partial: noise mainly widens CIs (~1 order of magnitude) and raises the ratio level, with only weak, logarithmic α̂ change. Text says σ swept 0.01–100, but figure legends show 0–3.162.

source_check.correct: V3: observed where identifiable. V7: partial. Noise chiefly widens uncertainty and raises the ratio level, with weak exponent changes; the ratio remains roughly constant with compute. Excessive noise produces NaNs, and Â and α̂ are nearly unidentifiable at σ = 3.162.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.4; Figure 4 bottom row; Figure 5 bottom right.
source_check.problem: The shared observed state overstates V7 dependence and requires an identifiability qualification for V3.

rows.operation_detail: Refit after applying log-normal noise independently to parameter counts.

rows.value: Fits with too much noise produce NaNs; at σ = 3.162, Â and α̂ are nearly unidentifiable.

relationships.condition: Three real parameter-count interpretations; multiplicative and log-normal-noise perturbations where fits are identifiable
relationships.reason: Compute-optimal tokens/parameter stays ≈20 and flat with compute, so N and D grow roughly equally (R2, R3, R4, R5, R11).
relationships.display_finding: The optimal ratio stayed near 20 tokens per parameter without appreciable compute dependence, implying roughly equal parameter and token growth.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Three real parameter-count interpretations; multiplicative and log-normal-noise perturbations where fits are identifiable
source_check.reason: R2–R5 and R11 preserve an approximately flat ratio with compute, consistent with roughly equal parameter and token growth. Approximately 20 applies to ordinary definitions; perturbations can shift the ratio level.

relationships.condition: Synthetic additive-constant and size-dependent systematic-bias errors in parameter counts
relationships.reason: With these errors the ratio trends up or down with compute, so equal growth holds only if counts are free of such errors (R7–R10).
relationships.display_finding: Additive and size-dependent parameter-measurement errors produced increasing or decreasing token-to-parameter ratios, distorting inferred equal growth.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Synthetic additive-constant and size-dependent systematic-bias errors in parameter counts
source_check.reason: R7–R10 show synthetic counting errors changing the ratio's compute trend, qualifying the Chinchilla equal-growth prescription under those errors.

relationships.condition: Three real parameter-count definitions (reported, standard formula, best fit; up to 15.2% apart)
relationships.reason: None of the five fit parameters differs significantly, and the ratio stays ≈20; counting choice did not shift the law here (R1–R4).
relationships.display_finding: Despite parameter definitions differing by up to 15.2%, none of the five fitted parameters differed significantly, and the ratio stayed near 20.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Three real parameter-count definitions (reported, standard formula, best fit; up to 15.2% apart)
source_check.reason: R1–R4 show no significant fitted-parameter differences and a ratio remaining around 20, challenging material counting dependence for this specific intervention.

relationships.condition: Synthetic additive-constant (e.g., embedding inclusion) and systematic-bias perturbations
relationships.reason: α̂ moves from 0.199 to 0.481 across additive constants, α̂ ∝ s^−1 under bias, and the optimal-ratio trend changes sign (R7–R10).
relationships.display_finding: Additive constants move α̂ from 0.199 to 0.481, systematic bias gives α̂ proportional to s^−1, and the optimal-ratio trend changes sign.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Synthetic additive-constant (e.g., embedding inclusion) and systematic-bias perturbations
source_check.reason: R7–R10 demonstrate fitted-exponent and allocation-trend dependence on synthetic counting changes. The additive exponent range spans the entire negative-to-positive sweep; embedding inclusion is a motivating analogy.

relationships.reason: α̂ and the ratio's flat trend are unchanged. Only the ratio level shifts (multiplicative), or uncertainty widens with a weak α̂ drop (noise) (R5, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Multiplicative perturbations preserved α̂ and the ratio's flat trend while shifting its level; log-normal noise widened uncertainty and weakly reduced α̂ while preserving the flat trend.

source_check.reason: R5 and R11 show conditional robustness of exponents and the approximately flat allocation trend, alongside ratio-level changes and increased uncertainty; dependence is incomplete.
